blocks.x: What Manitoba has done

Manitoba's new clinics, listed on the province's [New Clinics Are Open](https://gov.mb.ca/newclinics/index.html) page, offer evening and weekend hours and same-day care for illnesses, injuries and other health needs. In Winnipeg, the list in early November 2026 included:
**Misericordia Health Centre Minor Injury and Illness Clinic** (99 Cornish Avenue), open 7:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, marked as new.
**Minor Treatment Clinic at Health Sciences Centre** (700 William Avenue), open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily.
**Extended-hours primary care clinics** at Grace, Concordia and Victoria hospitals, open weekday evenings and weekend afternoons and evenings.
A Brandon clinic was also listed, and the province said more clinics were coming. Hours can change, so check the province's page before you visit.

Separately, Global News reported in June 2026 that the [Portage Place redevelopment](https://globalnews.ca/news/11936863/portage-place-grocery-store/) downtown included plans for a health-care centre.
What extended-hours care asks of a building

The province said these clinics are there for same-day care when your regular provider isn't available, or if you don't have one. Care delivered this way, over longer hours, asks more of a building. Clinics like these need space that supports:
**Longer operating hours,** with durable finishes and good security.
**High patient volumes,** with efficient flow from entry to exam room to exit.
**Accessibility,** for patients with mobility challenges.
**Frequent cleaning,** with cleanable surfaces, as the clinic's own policies and designer specify.
**Team-based care,** with spaces for physicians, nurse practitioners and other providers.

The Winnipeg sites on the province's list in early November 2026 were hospitals and health centres, so those sites alone did not show demand for leased clinic space. Private clinics, pharmacies, physiotherapy practices and other providers in neighbourhood plazas, offices and mixed-use buildings can face similar needs.
Our view: medical space can be a renovation opportunity for landlords

With [Winnipeg office vacancy](https://www.cbre.com/insights/figures/winnipeg-office-figures-q3-2026) at 15.1% (CBRE, Q3 2026), a landlord with empty space may want to consider medical tenants. But those tenants need space that meets specific requirements.
**Medical clinic renovation** in a former office or retail space typically involves:
**Interior demolition** of existing fit-outs.
**New layouts** with exam rooms, treatment rooms, waiting areas and staff spaces.
**Cleanable, durable flooring** such as sheet vinyl or commercial LVP.
**Durable, cleanable paint** finishes.
**Wider doors and accessible entrances.**
**Plumbing, electrical and ventilation work**, with permits applied for by City-licensed contractors.
**Permits,** including a building permit application and an [occupancy permit](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) if the use changes or the alterations are substantial.
Designing for extended hours
Clinics open evenings and weekends need extra attention to:
**Security:** well-lit entrances, secure doors and controlled access after hours.
**Durability:** finishes that withstand more hours of use.
**Wayfinding:** clear signage for patients unfamiliar with the clinic.
**Comfort:** waiting areas that work for longer waits.
A checklist for landlords and clinic operators
Confirm zoning and permitted uses for the space.
Check accessibility at entrances, washrooms and corridors.
Plan for plumbing in exam rooms.
Assess floor and wall finishes for cleanability.
In an older building, have suspect materials [tested for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before demolition.
Budget realistically: exam-room plumbing, power and ventilation can go beyond a standard office fit-out.
Allow time for permits and specialty trades.
What to watch

Watch for announcements of additional clinics under the province's initiative, and for any changes in how primary care is funded and delivered. If new Winnipeg locations move beyond hospital sites, that would say more about demand for leased space.
Converting office or retail space into a medical clinic

Former office and retail spaces can make good clinics, but the conversion has to address several issues. Ground-floor space is usually best for accessibility. Exam rooms need plumbing for sinks, which can be expensive if the space lacks nearby plumbing lines. Ceilings, floors and walls should be easy to clean, to the specification your clinical policies and designer set.
Ventilation requirements may also differ from office use. And a change of use means a building permit application first, then an occupancy permit.

Assessing these issues before signing a lease helps landlords and clinic operators avoid costly surprises. It also gives both sides a clear basis for negotiating who pays for which improvements, and how the cost is reflected in rent or tenant allowances. This is general information, not legal advice: have a lawyer review the lease, and confirm permits with the City.
The bottom line

Manitoba's push for evening, weekend and same-day care shows what clinic space has to do: run longer hours, move patients efficiently and stay accessible. The Winnipeg sites listed in early November 2026 were hospitals and health centres, so landlords should test demand for their own space before investing. Clinics designed for flow, durability and accessibility serve patients better.
